questions.prompt: How do you read `T extends U ? X : Y`?

options.text: If T is assignable to U, the type is X; otherwise it's Y — a type-level ternary

questions.explanation: A conditional type is a type-level ternary: if T is assignable to U the result is X, otherwise Y.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that conditional types distribute over unions?

options.text: A naked `T extends ...` is applied to each union member separately, and the results are unioned together
They only work on the first member

questions.explanation: When the checked type is a naked type parameter, the conditional applies to each member of a union and unions the results.

questions.prompt: Inside an `extends` clause, the ______ keyword captures part of the matched type, e.g. T extends (infer U)[] ? U : T. (one word)
questions.explanation: infer declares a type variable inside the extends clause to capture part of the matched type for use in the true branch.

questions.prompt: How do you extract a function's return type with a conditional?

options.text: F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never

questions.explanation: Matching the function shape and inferring R after => extracts the return type — essentially how the built-in ReturnType works.

questions.prompt: How do you stop a conditional type from distributing over a union?

options.text: Wrap both sides in a one-element tuple: [T] extends [U] ? ... : ...

questions.explanation: Wrapping in [T]/[U] prevents distribution, testing the whole type at once — the standard trick for detecting never, for instance.

questions.prompt: In a distributive conditional, what happens to members that resolve to `never`?

options.text: They drop out of the resulting union — which is how filtering (e.g. Exclude) works

questions.explanation: never members disappear from a union, so a conditional that maps unwanted members to never effectively filters them out.
